findings.reason: The protected app and immutable native sources initialize the first window with sum(data[:ones]). Python list slicing materializes k references, so those implementations use O(k) auxiliary space and do not meet the Optimal branch's required O(1) bound. candidate.py traverses those positions through a generator over range(ones), retaining constant-sized iterator and accumulator state while leaving the accepted algorithm unchanged.

On a legal 100000-element alternating array with k = 50000, repeated tracemalloc measurements found a minimum peak of 400076 bytes for both protected and native sources versus 540 bytes for the candidate, a 740.9x reduction. The input array was allocated before tracing, all implementations returned the same result, and no input mutation occurred, directly confirming the slice allocation the candidate removes.

The candidate preserves the recognizable fixed-width sliding window while making its state explicit through zeros_in_window and minimum_swaps. position clearly denotes first-window traversal and right denotes the entering boundary. The implementation is concise, conventional, free of unnecessary abstraction, and materially more faithful to its stated space bound than the protected source.

If k ones are to be contiguous, their final block has exactly k positions. For any chosen length-k window, its zeros equal the ones outside it, and each arbitrary-position swap pairs one such zero with one outside one. The candidate measures that cost for the first window, updates it exactly by removing the departing value and adding the entering value, and retains the minimum over every possible block. Returning zero for k at most one is correct.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode algorithm problem 1151, Python, and native entrypoint Solution.minSwaps. Authenticated source evidence confirms a binary array, grouping all ones in any location, three explained examples, length range 1 through 10^5, binary element values, and six hints. The candidate preserves solve(data), arbitrary-position swap semantics demonstrated by the examples, and the integer minimum-swap result.

The immutable native source remains bound to verified submission 2067852416 and is unchanged. Native, protected, and candidate sources use the same total-one count, at-most-one early return, first-window zero count, sliding update, running minimum, and result. The candidate changes only the first-window traversal and descriptive state names, so its algorithm and data flow remain aligned with the Accepted implementation while fixing app-local auxiliary space.

The candidate counts ones once, traverses the first length-k window once, and slides through the remaining positions once, establishing O(n) time. It stores only scalar counts, boundaries, and generator state, establishing O(1) auxiliary space. This meets both manifest bounds; the protected slice is the only reason the current app source does not.

The unchanged hidden tiers scale alternating arrays from 64 through 256 to 512 elements while keeping k linear in n. The exact candidate passed all 10 ordinary cases, all three benchmark outputs, and scaling at a 1.66x largest runtime ratio and +0.14 relative growth exponent; three additional consecutive runs also passed between +0.12 and +0.15. An independently correct window-recount control passed every output but failed only scaling at 143.82x and +1.46.

The Approach accurately derives the fixed block length k, the equivalence between window zeros and required swaps, first-window initialization, constant-time adjacent-window updates, and minimization over all placements. Its O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary-space claims are true for candidate.py, and its alternatives and edge cases cover recounting, simulation, no ones, one one, all ones, and arbitrary rather than adjacent swaps.
